messages.subject: Re: Getting error PipeMapRed.waitOutputThreads() while running mapreduce program for 40mb of sizedataset
messages.subject_clean: Getting error PipeMapRed.waitOutputThreads() while running mapreduce program for 40mb of sizedataset
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am sure you read the error messages carefully so you already know it's a memory issue. So the options are to try and use less or try and have more available. It is common for hadoop systems to be configured so that the available memory is split between the max number of tasks allowed. Since the assumption is  that those tasks are implemented in java, the slice of memory is allocated to the each JVM, so that the memory size of all the JVMs running at any given time doesn't exceed the physically available memory. But if you are running RHadoop, each map or reduce tasks has two processes (actually in some instances three, but the third has very modest memory requirements). The java process is an instance of hadoop streaming. It is not memory intensive and can be configured to use tens of MBs. The rest can be made available for the R process. So the idea is to have hadoop configured, or possibly a RHadoop queue in a multi-use system, so that al the JVMS that can run at once use, say 10 to 15% of available memory and the rest is available for R.  This is to try and have more memory available. To try and use less, this failure is so early in the map code that it shouldn't have anything to deal with the code of the map function. It could be though that you are using lots of memory on the "master" instance from which you are calling mapreduce, and the environment is automatically replicated on the nodes. So let's say if you were loading 40MB of data locally and you call mapreduce, those 40mbs will be replicated all over the cluster and loaded as soon as the map or reduce processes start. It could be that this is fine on your master instance, but not on the slaves because, for instance, they are configured to run 10 maps and 10 reduces at the same time, and all together they exceed memory resources. If this is a multi tenant system, it's also important to know what other workloads are present on the system at the same time. For short, this seems to me like a system resources problems and you should troubleshoot it as such, that is try to ssh into one of the clients, if it is allowed, and monitor all processes with top and see what's using up memory compared to what your expectations are. If ssh is not allowed your sysadming will have some other monitoring in place such as Ganglia or related and may be able to help you monitor one failing instance. I hope this helps

Antonio

messages.subject: Re: Error while inserting to HBase table: RHBase
messages.subject_clean: Error while inserting to HBase table: RHBase
messages.body_plain:
Hi
what version of rhbase are you running and what serialization options did you specify, if any, in hb.init? We changed (fixed) the naming of serialization options and it could be that  that is creating problems with pre-existing data. I  googled your error message and Prof. Brian Ripley himself says

"For the record, this sort of message almost always indicates internal
corruption of R objects, so run the example under valgrind. "

The reporter of the error eventually said that after recreating his data from scratch the error went away. Not to say this is not a bug in RHbase, but it's a possibility.

Antonio

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#989] randomForest in RHadoop
messages.body_plain:
It could be a time out. You need to dig into the logs to figure out what it is exactly. You could also put some debugging calls in your program to see where it fails. If you suspect call xyz() to cause the problem, you could add:

rmr.str("about to call xyz")
xyz()
rmr.str("done with xyz")

Then you can examine the stderr logs to see if the failure happens before or after xyz.
To avoid time outs you just need to call status("some message") every few seconds. If the time out happens in a library call you can't modify and if it has an option to write a progress bar or some such, you can turn that on while at the same time surrounding it  with a sink call as follows

sink(stderr())
long_library_call(...., verbose = TRUE)
sink(NULL)

I hope this helps.

Antonio

On Thu, Sep 26, 2013 at 9:33 AM, Krishna Gajula <kgaju...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

>
> I am pretty new to rmr2. I have couple of questions about predictive modeling using rmr2 (e.g. Using NN or decision tree algorithm).
>
> 1. In R stand alone mode creating, training and re-training predictive models is pretty straight forward. You save the model to the disk using save(), move it to the location where you would like to test it and load it using load(). How does it work in rmr2 world ? Do we need to save models on HDFS ? Any examples on how this can be implemented ?

I think you need to look at rmr2 as an Hadoop equivalent of foreach or other parallel library. It provides you with a building block but not a complete solution. If you need to create multiple models on chunks of data that fit into main memory, you can do something like this

> from.dfs(mapreduce(to.dfs(mtcars),map = function(k,v) keyval(v$cyl, v), reduce = function(k, vv) keyval(k, list(lm(mpg~carb + disp, data=vv)))))
$key
[1] 6 4 8

$val
$val[[1]]

Call:
lm(formula = mpg ~ carb + disp, data = vv)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)         carb         disp
   12.15971      0.63168      0.02955

$val[[2]]

Call:
lm(formula = mpg ~ carb + disp, data = vv)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)         carb         disp
    39.6345       2.2747      -0.1568

$val[[3]]

Call:
lm(formula = mpg ~ carb + disp, data = vv)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)         carb         disp
   23.82567     -0.59733     -0.01879

If instead of reading the output into main memory you want to save it to HDFS, just drop the from.dfs and check the output option to mapreduce. If you need to solve a really large modeling problem, you will need to come up with your own algorithms that may also use rmr2, but won't fit the body of this email. The hope is that the community will fill the gap using rmr2 as a starting point. One example for random forests can be found here

http://blog.cloudera.com/blog/2013/02/how-to-resample-from-a-large-data-set-in-parallel-with-r-on-hadoop/

>
> 2. How can we we perform different operations like combining, chaining and composition of models in rmr?

Can you define these terms for the uninitiated and show some examples on small data?

>
> 3. Can we create PMML models from the rmr models ?

There is no such a thing as rmr models. Using the  package pmml, we can modify the above code as

from.dfs(mapreduce(to.dfs(mtcars),map = function(k,v) keyval(v$cyl, v), reduce = function(k, vv) keyval(k, list(pmml(lm(mpg~carb + disp, data=vv))))))

and produce pmml.

I think you need to moderate your expectations as far as rmr2. It is just a package focused on one type of parallel programming, in the mold of foreach or snow. It's not a replacement for the R system, not a parallel version of the R system, doesn't provide parallel versions of any of the thousands of R packages and so on. It is just one package. There are proprietary products out there that will provide some large scale model fitting capabilities, but it's a trade off between convenience and power (besides the OSS/ proprietary issue).

Antonio

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#994] Predictive modeling using RHadoop
messages.body_plain:
Well you are asking an ambiguous question (what does "leverage" mean exactly?)  for some 4000 packages, so the answer is yes and no, but you knew that already. More concretely, you can install any R package on your cluster and make calls from inside the map and reduce functions. That is true in general, with the exception of packages or functions that read or write their data only to files (for instance, graphics devices) or others that will write to stdout no matter what one does. In both cases there are things one can do to work around these problems and make them compatible anyway, and depending how much effort you are going to put in and how much performance penalty you are willing to tolerate, you may very well get close to 100% compatibility. For instance, if you need to generate images in a mapreduce job, you could let graphical devices write to a file, read the file back into memory and return some representation of its content as return value of a map function, or you may be able to use a binary connection and get the image written to a raw vector, I am not sure. So in this sense, mostR packages, where "most" is experience-based, not a statistical estimate, are compatible.  The ones that may be beyond any attempt to integrate are parallel programming packages, but one would be hard pressed to find a good reason to use them within a map function. There may be other unforseen sources of incompatibility, we don't have a survey or anything systematic. So let's say you want to use rlm in a map or reduce function, you would just need to install  MASS to the cluster, then you can write something like

mapreduce(..., map = function(k,v) keyval(v$userid, v), reduce = function(k,v) keyval(k, list(rlm(some.formula, data = v))))

or some such, this is not real code. The idea is, use the map to preprocess and split the data, then call rlm on the splits. So these are the good news. The bad news are if you need to solve one big problem. No natural split in the data exists or is desired and a single overall model is sought. Then you have to come up with your own algorithm, as in the random forest case. It makes use of a variety of existing packages, but it is a new algorithm. You can't just write rlm(some.formula, data = big.data.in.HDFS). It would be nice, but there is no shortcut, the algorithms will have to be written, that is true whether you are talking about R or Java or anything. Of course there may be a sudden breakthrough, I am just saying that it would be very big and unexpected. What rmr2 is hoping to achieve is making the writing of this new generation of algorithms more productive and more focused on the logic and less on the nitty-gritty.

Antonio

messages.subject: Introducing plyrmr
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
this is to announce a preview-level availability of a new package, plyrmr. It builds on top of rmr2 to provide an easier, data frame focused approach to writing mapreduce programs. An expression in plyrmr may look like this:

```
output(transform(input("big/data/set/"), ratio = col1/col2), "some/directory")

```

As the name suggests, this work is inspired by `plyr` (many thanks to Hadley for fruitful discussions) but combines other types of data frame processing from other packages and some of its own. Head over to our wiki <https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/RHadoop/wiki/plyrmr> for details. We are releasing this early to get feedback to help us improve the package. That means that not everything is in place, in particular you need to build plyrmr from source and rmr2 from the dev branch to get things going. It's all explained in the wiki, but just so that you don't get disappointed.  There is a tutorial and also the help function will return useful info, but still a little unpolished. A first release is in the works. Please kick the tires and let us know what you think. Post your examples, questions and what not here. For issues that require a resolution you can also use the plyrmr issue tracker. Thanks

Antonio

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#994] Predictive modeling using RHadoop
messages.body_plain:
Thank you again Antonio for great explanation! It clearly makes sense to use rmr2 for parallel model building with the help of R packages that can work on small chunk of data available to the given mapper or reducer and take resulting models out of Hadoop for scoring in more real-time fashion or for visualization purpose. Just like how pig or Hive abstracts out all the complexities of mapreduce programming from developers, hopefully it will get easier for data scientists/R programmers not to have deal with MapReduce complexities. Howerver rmr2 is a great help for them to code using familiar R syntax today.

On Friday, September 27, 2013 11:34:05 AM UTC-5, Antonio Piccolboni wrote:
> Well you are asking an ambiguous question (what does "leverage" mean exactly?)  for some 4000 packages, so the answer is yes and no, but you knew that already. More concretely, you can install any R package on your cluster and make calls from inside the map and reduce functions. That is true in general, with the exception of packages or functions that read or write their data only to files (for instance, graphics devices) or others that will write to stdout no matter what one does. In both cases there are things one can do to work around these problems and make them compatible anyway, and depending how much effort you are going to put in and how much performance penalty you are willing to tolerate, you may very well get close to 100% compatibility. For instance, if you need to generate images in a mapreduce job, you could let graphical devices write to a file, read the file back into memory and return some representation of its content as return value of a map function, or you may be able to use a binary connection and get the image written to a raw vector, I am not sure. So in this sense, mostR packages, where "most" is experience-based, not a statistical estimate, are compatible.  The ones that may be beyond any attempt to integrate are parallel programming packages, but one would be hard pressed to find a good reason to use them within a map function. There may be other unforseen sources of incompatibility, we don't have a survey or anything systematic. So let's say you want to use rlm in a map or reduce function, you would just need to install  MASS to the cluster, then you can write something like
>
> mapreduce(..., map = function(k,v) keyval(v$userid, v), reduce = function(k,v) keyval(k, list(rlm(some.formula, data = v))))
>
> or some such, this is not real code. The idea is, use the map to preprocess and split the data, then call rlm on the splits. So these are the good news. The bad news are if you need to solve one big problem. No natural split in the data exists or is desired and a single overall model is sought. Then you have to come up with your own algorithm, as in the random forest case. It makes use of a variety of existing packages, but it is a new algorithm. You can't just write rlm(some.formula, data = big.data.in.HDFS). It would be nice, but there is no shortcut, the algorithms will have to be written, that is true whether you are talking about R or Java or anything. Of course there may be a sudden breakthrough, I am just saying that it would be very big and unexpected. What rmr2 is hoping to achieve is making the writing of this new generation of algorithms more productive and more focused on the logic and less on the nitty-gritty.
>
>
> Antonio
>
>
>
> On Fri, Sep 27, 2013 at 8:18 AM, Krishna Gajula <kgaju...@gmail.com> wrote:

I do agree that RHadoop is not a complete solution, but I was trying to understand it's architecture and capabilities so I can leverage it along with other technologies to build a solution for our predictive analysis needs. Random forest example is very helpful to understand how to build models in parallel fashion with Poisson distribution sampling and re-sampling. It helps everybody who is considering rmr2 for their production environment. I have one follow up question though.
